title: Avogadro's number
textbookText: 13.5 One Mole One mole is a unit for the measurement of a quantity of a substance in terms of volume or mass. A mole corresponds to the mass of a substance that contains 6.02 × 1023 particles of the substance. In other words, one mole is the mass of as much as the number of atoms present in 12 gm of carbon–12 isotope because 12 gm of carbon–12 contains 6.02 × 1023 number of carbon–12 atoms. The molecular weight of a substance expressed in gram is called one mole. Mole is not a number but it is quantity. Mole is a basic unit of SI system and symbol ‘mol’ is assigned to this. Mass of one mole of any substance is known as molar mass. For hydrogen gas, molecular weight is 2 and molar mass is 2 gm. Therefore, Molar mass of hydrogen = 1mole of hydrogen = 2gm of hydrogen = Mass of 6.02×1023 hydrogen molecules Molar mass of oxygen=1 mole of oxygen = 32 gm of oxygen= Mass of 6.02 × 1023 oxygen molecules Molar mass of water = 1 mole of water = 18 gm of water = Mass of 6.02 × 1023 water molecules If m is the total mass of a gas in a container, and M is its molar mass then, number of mole n = m M . 13.6 Avogadro's Law Statement: “Under identical condition of temperature and pressure, equal volume of all gases contains the equal number of molecules.” If we take 1 mole of a gas at NTP then, any gas has equal volume 22.4l = 22.4 × 10–3 m3 and hence contains equal number of molecules 6.02 × 1023. For example, at NTP, 1 mole of hydrogen gas (2 gram of hydrogen) occupies the volume of 22.4l, and contains 6.02 × 1023 molecules of hydrogen. Similarly, 1 mole of oxygen gas (32 gram of oxygen) occupies the volume of 22.4l, and contains 6.02 × 1023 molecules of oxygen.

Avogadro's number Avogadro's number is the number of molecules present in one mole of a gas at NTP. It is the same for all gases, and is equal to 6.02 × 1023 molecules. It is denoted by NA. For example; 1 mole of H2 gas contains 6.02 × 1023H2 molecules 1 mole of O2 gas contains 6.02 × 1023 O2 molecules, etc. Importance of Avogadro’s Number NA 1. To calculate the number of molecules present in a given volume of gas. 2. To calculate the number of atoms present in a given amount of substance. 3. To calculate the number of molecules present in a given amount of substance. 4. To calculate the weight of one atom of an element. 5. To calculate the weight of one molecule of a substance.
